title: Gender-Based Violence (GBV)
path: Overview of Reproductive Health and Rights
Gender Dynamics, Gender-Based Violence (GBV), and Harmful Traditional Practices

headings.title: Understanding Gender-Based Violence
headings.content: Gender-based violence refers to any harmful act directed against an individual based on socially ascribed differences between males and females. Rooted in systemic power imbalances, this form of violence violates fundamental human rights and affects individuals across all demographics, though women and girls bear the heaviest burden globally and locally. In Nigerian communities, traditional expectations around male dominance and female subservience often normalize coercive behaviors. Midwives must recognize that GBV is never merely a private domestic dispute but a major public health emergency requiring professional intervention and institutional response.

headings.title: Socio-Cultural Drivers and Vulnerabilities in Nigeria
headings.content: Cultural norms, religious misinterpretations, and economic dependency heavily shape vulnerability to violence in Nigeria. Patriarchy often grants men absolute authority over household decisions, restricting female autonomy and financial independence. When women lack independent sources of income, leaving an abusive environment becomes nearly impossible. Furthermore, silence is frequently enforced by family elders who prioritize preserving family reputation over the safety of the victim. Midwives practicing in resource-constrained settings frequently encounter patients trapped by these deep-seated traditions.

headings.title: Forms of Gender-Based Violence
headings.content: Gender-based violence manifests in multiple overlapping ways. Physical violence involves acts resulting in bodily harm or trauma. Sexual violence encompasses non-consensual sexual contact, marital rape, and forced impregnation. Psychological abuse relies on threats, isolation, and constant humiliation, which erodes self-esteem. Economic abuse deprives a partner of financial resources or controls access to employment. In addition, harmful traditional practices such as female genital mutilation and forced child marriage represent institutionalized forms of GBV deeply embedded in specific cultures.

headings.title: Clinical and Psychosocial Impact
headings.content: The consequences of gender-based violence extend far beyond immediate physical injuries. Survivors frequently present with chronic pelvic pain, recurrent sexually transmitted infections, unintended pregnancies, and obstetric fistula resulting from forced or traumatic intercourse. Psychologically, survivors suffer from depression, severe anxiety, post-traumatic stress disorder, and suicidal ideation. Stigma and shame often cause patients to delay seeking care, worsening both physical ailments and mental health struggles.

headings.title: The Role of the Midwife in Identification and Screening
headings.content: Midwives occupy a privileged frontline position because pregnant and postpartum women visit antenatal and postnatal clinics regularly. Routine screening during booking visits allows midwives to uncover hidden trauma. Key indicators include unexplained injuries, late-stage presentation for antenatal care, overly controlling partners who refuse to leave the examination room, and symptoms of severe anxiety or depression. Asking direct, compassionate questions in a private setting is essential for successful disclosure.

headings.title: Trauma-Informed Care and Patient Support
headings.content: Trauma-informed care shifts the clinical question from "What is wrong with you?" to "What happened to you?" This approach prioritizes physical and emotional safety, trustworthiness, transparency, and patient empowerment. Midwives must create a non-judgmental environment, practice active listening, and respect patient autonomy at every step. Pressuring a survivor to take legal action before they are ready can re-traumatize them. Instead, support must center on validating their feelings and respecting their personal timeline.

headings.title: Legal Frameworks, Referrals, and Multidisciplinary Management
headings.content: Managing gender-based violence effectively requires a coordinated multidisciplinary team consisting of midwives, doctors, social workers, legal aid organizations, and law enforcement. In Nigeria, legislation such as the Violence Against Persons Prohibition Act provides vital legal protections, though enforcement varies across states. Midwives must understand local referral pathways to connect survivors with safe housing, psychological counseling, and legal assistance. Comprehensive documentation of injuries with the patient's consent is crucial should legal proceedings follow.
